items.title: Intelligent routing with llm-d
items.lead: How a request finds a vLLM pod, and why routing to the pod that already holds the right KV cache is faster.

points: A vLLM pod holds the model weights, a KV cache of work it has already computed, and a waiting queue for requests it cannot run yet.
When traffic rises against one pod, the queue fills and the cache alone cannot keep up, so the work spreads across several pods.
The Endpoint Picker filters the pods, scores each one, and the highest total wins.
The score favors a pod that already holds the right cache, so that pod serves the request faster.

items.title: Managing LLM traffic at scale
items.bridge: Routing gets a request to the right pod. Next, look inside that pod at what serves it.
items.lead: Inside a vLLM pod: model weights, the KV cache, and the waiting queue, and what happens when traffic climbs.

details.summary: Why one pod is not enough
points: The pod keeps what it has already computed, so a repeat prompt starts warm from the KV cache.
The cache grows with every token, and most of what arrives has already been computed as a shared prefix.
When work arrives faster than one pod can finish it, a second replica runs in parallel and builds its own cache.
A cache-blind load balancer sees only connection counts, so it can send a request to a cold replica that recomputes the prefill.

items.title: Requests share long prefixes
items.bridge: The pod reuses cache when it can. Next, see why requests share cache in the first place.
items.lead: Why so many requests carry the same opening tokens, and how a shared prefix turns into cache you can reuse.

details.summary: How a shared prefix becomes reusable cache
points: Requests carry the same shared instructions ahead of the user's own question, so they share a long opening prefix.
That prefix hashes into blocks the pod can look up in its KV cache index.
Without cache-aware routing, every pod prefills the same prefix from scratch each time.
llm-d sends the request to the pod that already holds the prefix, which cuts cost and latency.

items.title: The objects you kubectl apply
items.bridge: That covers how llm-d serves a request. Next, the Kubernetes objects you apply to make it run.
items.lead: An overview of how Gateway, HTTPRoute, and InferencePool wire together into the thing that serves traffic.

details.summary: The objects and the three layers they sit in
points: Gateway API supplies Gateway, which accepts incoming requests, and HTTPRoute, which sends /v1/chat/completions to the pool.
The Gateway API Inference Extension adds InferencePool, which gathers the matching model servers.
The llm-d install adds the Endpoint Picker that picks a server, its Service, and the optional InferenceObjective that sets request priority.
The model server pods, labeled app=vllm, run the model on the GPU, so one address routes to many pods.

items.title: Inside HTTPRoute and InferencePool
items.bridge: You have seen the objects at a glance. Next, open up the two that route a request to the pods.
items.lead: What HTTPRoute and InferencePool each do, and how they hand a request from the URL path to the model server pods.

details.summary: How HTTPRoute and InferencePool hand off a request
points: HTTPRoute matches requests by a path prefix and optional headers, so /v1/chat/completions requests go to the InferencePool named in its backendRefs.
InferencePool is a label rule; its selector matchLabels picks the model server pods, and targetPorts names the port they serve on.
The pool's endpointPickerRef names the Endpoint Picker and the port it answers on.
The Endpoint Picker scores the endpoints for each request and returns the chosen endpoint address.

items.label: 1.5 · Part 1
items.title: Inside HTTPRoute
items.bridge: Now take each object on its own, starting with HTTPRoute.
items.lead: A closer look at HTTPRoute on its own: how it matches a request by path prefix and headers and points it at a backend.

details.summary: How HTTPRoute matches and forwards a request
points: HTTPRoute routes a URL path to a pool of model servers by matching requests on a path prefix.
Its parentRefs attach it to the inference-gateway, so the Gateway hands it matching traffic.
The match handles only paths starting with /v1/chat/completions.
Its backendRefs name an InferencePool, so each matched request goes to an available model server pod.

items.label: 1.5 · Part 2
items.title: Inside InferencePool
items.bridge: HTTPRoute points at an InferencePool. Next, open up what that is.
items.lead: What InferencePool declares, and how the Endpoint Picker routes a request to a ready pod using policies and live metrics like queue depth and cache use.

points: InferencePool is a label rule that selects the model server pods, and the port they serve on.
The Endpoint Picker watches the pool for that rule and the pods for members, keeping one entry for each ready endpoint.
It scrapes queue depth and cache use from each endpoint and routes on policies plus those metrics.
The pool declares the members; the picker keeps the ready list.

items.label: 1.6 · Part 1
items.title: Inside InferenceObjective
items.bridge: The pool decides where a request goes. InferenceObjective decides which requests matter most.
items.lead: What an InferenceObjective declares, and how the Endpoint Picker reads the priority for a request from the objective named in the header.

points: An InferenceObjective consists of a name, a pool, and a priority.
Each request selects one InferenceObjective: the x-llm-d-inference-objective header maps to the metadata.name.
The Endpoint Picker reads the InferenceObjective and acts on the priority; an unset priority is treated as 0.
The higher the value, the more critical the request. Negative values are sheddable, rejected under saturation. An InferencePool can serve many objectives.

items.label: Reference
items.title: The Kubernetes objects behind llm-d
items.lead: A reference pass over every object llm-d relies on and how they relate.

points: Gateway API holds the Gateway where every request arrives and the HTTPRoute that sends /v1/chat/completions to the pool.
The Gateway API Inference Extension holds the InferencePool, the group of servers to route to, and the InferenceObjective that marks which requests matter most.
The llm-d install holds the Endpoint Picker pod that picks the least busy server and the Service that gives the pool its address.
The LLM inference service holds the model server pods, labeled app=vllm, that run the model on the GPU.

sections.title: Flow control
sections.blurb: How llm-d admits, queues, and paces requests under load.

details.summary: How the Endpoint Picker paces requests
points: The Endpoint Picker sits between the Gateway and the model server pods, deciding which endpoint each request goes to.
It reads live signals from every pod, queue depth and cache use, so it can tell a busy endpoint from a ready one.
When every endpoint is saturated, flow control holds the request rather than piling it onto a full queue.
As capacity frees up, held requests are released to the endpoint that can serve them fastest.
